questions.prompt: A rectangle has perimeter 34 cm. Its length is 3 cm greater than its width. Use simultaneous equations to find both dimensions.
questions.solution: Let length be l and width be w. l + w = 17 and l − w = 3. Add: 2l = 20, so l = 10 cm and w = 7 cm.

questions.prompt: A student suggests x = 6, y = 3 solves (1) 2x + y = 13 and (2) x − y = 2. Test the suggestion and find the correct solution.
questions.solution: The proposed pair gives 15 in equation (1), not 13, so the claim fails. Multiply equation (1) by -1 and equation (2) by 1. Subtract the second NEW equation from the first: -3x = -15, so x = 5. Substitute x = 5 in equation (1) to obtain y = 3.
markPoints: B1 Test the proposed values correctly
M1 Explain why the proposal is invalid
M1 Use elimination to find a valid pair

questions.prompt: Explain why elimination can be used for (1) x + y = 5 and (2) 2x − y = 7. Then solve them.
questions.solution: The y terms have opposite coefficients, so adding the original equations eliminates y. Multiply equation (1) by -1 and equation (2) by 1. Subtract the second NEW equation from the first: -3x = -12, so x = 4. Substitute x = 4 in equation (1) to obtain y = 1.
markPoints: M1 Carry out a valid elimination

questions.prompt: Explain why elimination can be used for (1) x + y = 7 and (2) 2x − y = 8. Then solve them.

questions.prompt: At a cinema, 2 adult tickets and 1 child ticket cost £15. Another purchase of 1 adult ticket and 3 child tickets costs £15. Find each ticket price using simultaneous equations.
questions.solution: Let x and y be adult and child ticket prices. Equations: 2x + y = 15 and x + 3y = 15. Multiply equation (1) by 1 and equation (2) by 2. Subtract (2) from (1): -5y = -15, so y = 3. Substitute in 2x + y = 15: x = 6. Hence £6 and £3.
markPoints: M1 Solve for one ticket price

questions.prompt: Three notebooks and two pens cost £29. Two notebooks and four pens cost £30. Form simultaneous equations and find each price.
questions.solution: Let n and p be the prices. 3n + 2p = 29 and 2n + 4p = 30. Double the first: 6n + 4p = 58. Subtract the second: 4n = 28, so n = 7. Then p = 4. Prices: £7 and £4.

questions.prompt: At a theatre, 2 standard tickets and 1 concession ticket cost £21. Another purchase of 1 standard ticket and 3 concession tickets costs £23. Find each ticket price using simultaneous equations.
questions.solution: Let x and y be standard and concession ticket prices. Equations: 2x + y = 21 and x + 3y = 23. Multiply equation (1) by 1 and equation (2) by 2. Subtract (2) from (1): -5y = -25, so y = 5. Substitute in 2x + y = 21: x = 8. Hence £8 and £5.
markPoints: M1 Solve for one ticket price

questions.prompt: A collection contains 14 coins, each worth either 20p or 50p. Their total value is £5.20. Find the number of each coin using simultaneous equations.
questions.solution: Let a and b count 20p and 50p coins. a + b = 14 and 20a + 50b = 520. Subtract 20 times the first from the second: 30b = 240, so b = 8 and a = 6.

questions.prompt: At a science centre, 2 adult tickets and 1 child ticket cost £23. One adult ticket and 3 child tickets cost £19. Find both prices using simultaneous equations.
questions.solution: Let a and c be prices in pounds. 2a + c = 23 and a + 3c = 19. Double the second and subtract the first: 5c = 15. Thus c = 3 and a = 10.

questions.prompt: A bag contains 11 red or blue counters. Red counters score 3 points and blue counters score 5 points. The total score is 43. Find the number of counters of each colour.
questions.solution: r + b = 11 and 3r + 5b = 43. Subtract 3 times the first: 2b = 10, so b = 5 and r = 6.

questions.prompt:
Solve these equations by elimination, showing any equation you multiply before adding or subtracting:
(1) 2x + y = 6
(2) 3x + 2y = 9
questions.solution: Multiply equation (1) by 2 and equation (2) by 1. Subtract the second NEW equation from the first: 1x = 3, so x = 3. Substitute x = 3 in equation (1) to obtain y = 0.

questions.prompt: To solve 3x + 2y = 14 and 4x + 3y = 19, a pupil multiplies only the left side of the first equation by 3. Explain why this is wrong, then solve correctly by elimination.
questions.solution: Both sides must be multiplied to preserve equality. Multiply the first by 3 and the second by 2: 9x + 6y = 42 and 8x + 6y = 38. Subtract: x = 4. Then y = 1.
markPoints: B1 Both sides must be multiplied
M1 Correct pair of scaled equations

questions.prompt:
Solve these equations by elimination, showing any equation you multiply before adding or subtracting:
(1) 4x + y = 22
(2) 3x + 4y = 23
questions.solution: Multiply equation (1) by 4 and equation (2) by 1. Subtract the second NEW equation from the first: 13x = 65, so x = 5. Substitute x = 5 in equation (1) to obtain y = 2.

questions.prompt: Solve 2x + 2y = 18 and 4x + 2y = 30 by elimination. Explain why no multiplication is needed.
questions.solution: Subtract the first equation from the second: 2x = 12, so x = 6. Substitute to get y = 3. The y coefficients already match.

questions.prompt:

questions.solution: Multiply equation (1) by 3 and equation (2) by 1. Subtract the second NEW equation from the first: 6x = 42, so x = 7. Substitute x = 7 in equation (1) to obtain y = 4.

questions.prompt: An exam solution starts with 4x + 2y = 22 and x + 4y = 23. Solve the pair and substitute your answers back to check both equations.
questions.solution: Multiply equation (1) by 4 and equation (2) by 2. Subtract the second NEW equation from the first: 14x = 42, so x = 3. Substitute x = 3 in equation (1) to obtain y = 5. Check both equations: left sides are 22 and 23, equal to their right sides.

questions.prompt: An exam solution starts with 2x + 2y = 12 and x + 3y = 10. Solve the pair and substitute your answers back to check both equations.

questions.prompt: An exam solution starts with 3x + 2y = 21 and x + 4y = 17. Solve the pair and substitute your answers back to check both equations.
questions.solution: Multiply equation (1) by 4 and equation (2) by 2. Subtract the second NEW equation from the first: 10x = 50, so x = 5. Substitute x = 5 in equation (1) to obtain y = 3. Check both equations: left sides are 21 and 17, equal to their right sides.

questions.prompt: An exam solution starts with 4x + 2y = 32 and x + 3y = 18. Solve the pair and substitute your answers back to check both equations.

questions.prompt:
Solve by elimination and explain your choice of multipliers:
(1) 7x + 5y = 9
(2) 4x + 7y = 1
questions.solution: The chosen multipliers make the y coefficients equal. Multiply equation (1) by 7 and equation (2) by 5. Subtract the second NEW equation from the first: 29x = 58, so x = 2. Substitute x = 2 in equation (1) to obtain y = -1.
markPoints: M1 Explain a valid multiplier choice to eliminate a variable
M1 Obtain and solve one-variable equation

questions.prompt: Solve 2x + 3y = 8 and 3x − 2y = 4 by elimination. Give exact fractional answers.
questions.solution: Multiply the first by 2 and the second by 3, then add: 13x = 28, so x = 28/13. Substitute: 3y = 8 − 56/13 = 48/13, hence y = 16/13.

questions.prompt: The equations are 2x + 3y = 12 and 4x + 6y = k. Explain what happens when (a) k = 24 and (b) k = 25.
questions.solution: Twice the first equation is 4x + 6y = 24. (a) When k = 24 the equations are identical, so there are infinitely many solutions on 2x + 3y = 12. (b) When k = 25, subtraction gives 0 = 1, so there is no solution.
markPoints: B1 Infinitely many solutions for k = 24
M1 Obtain a contradiction for k = 25

questions.prompt: Solve the pair 0.5x + 1.5y = 0.5 and 1.5x − 0.5y = 1.5. Give exact values.
questions.solution: Multiply both equations by 2: x + 3y = 1 and 3x − y = 3. Multiply the second by 3, then add to the first: 10x = 10. Hence x = 1; substituting gives y = 0.
markPoints: M1 Clear decimals or use exact fractional coefficients

questions.prompt: Solve x/2 + y/3 = 4 and x/3 − y/2 = 1 by elimination. Give exact answers.
questions.solution: Multiply both equations by 6: 3x + 2y = 24 and 2x − 3y = 6. Multiply these by 3 and 2 and add: 13x = 84, so x = 84/13. Then 2y = 24 − 252/13 = 60/13, so y = 30/13.

questions.prompt: Solve the pair 0.5x + 1.5y = 4.5 and 1.5x − 0.5y = 3.5. Give exact values.
questions.solution: Multiply both equations by 2: x + 3y = 9 and 3x − y = 7. Multiply the second by 3, then add to the first: 10x = 30. Hence x = 3; substituting gives y = 2.
markPoints: M1 Clear decimals or use exact fractional coefficients

questions.prompt: At a show, adult tickets cost £8 and child tickets cost £5. Exactly 120 tickets are sold for £810. Find the number of each type sold.
questions.solution: a + c = 120 and 8a + 5c = 810. Subtract 5 times the first equation: 3a = 210. Thus a = 70 and c = 50.

questions.prompt: A pupil claims the solution of (1) 5x + 4y = 28 and (2) 2x + 3y = 14 is x=4, y=3. Decide if the claim is valid. Find the true solution by elimination.
questions.solution: The proposed pair gives 32 in equation (1), not 28, so the claim fails. Multiply equation (1) by 3 and equation (2) by 4. Subtract the second NEW equation from the first: 7x = 28, so x = 4. Substitute x = 4 in equation (1) to obtain y = 2.
markPoints: B1 Check claim in original equation

questions.prompt: A pupil says 3x + 5y = 30 and 3x + y = 18 have solution x = 5, y = 4. Explain why checking only one equation can never establish a simultaneous solution. Then find the correct pair.
questions.solution: A simultaneous solution must satisfy both equations. The proposed pair gives 35 rather than 30 in the first, so it fails. Subtract the second equation from the first: 4y = 12, so y = 3. Then 3x + 3 = 18, giving x = 5.
markPoints: B1 Reject the pair using a correct substitution

questions.prompt: A pupil claims the solution of (1) 4x + 4y = 40 and (2) 2x + 4y = 28 is x=6, y=5. Decide if the claim is valid. Find the true solution by elimination.
questions.solution: The proposed pair gives 44 in equation (1), not 40, so the claim fails. Multiply equation (1) by 4 and equation (2) by 4. Subtract the second NEW equation from the first: 8x = 48, so x = 6. Substitute x = 6 in equation (1) to obtain y = 4.
markPoints: B1 Check claim in original equation

questions.prompt: The equations are 5x + 5y = 60 and 3x + 5y = 46. (a) Solve by elimination. (b) Both right-hand sides are then increased by 10. Explain which variable stays unchanged and find the new solution.
questions.solution: Subtract: 2x = 14, so x = 7. Then y = 5. Adding 10 to both right sides leaves their difference unchanged, so x stays 7. The new first equation is 5x + 5y = 70, giving y = 7.
markPoints: B1 Difference unchanged so x stays 7
M1 Substitute into the new equation
